q: One end of a long horizontal rope is moved steadily up and down, and a wave travels along the rope. How do the particles of the rope move?
o: Along the rope together with the wave
Up and down about their mean positions
In circles around the axis of the rope
Back and forth along the length of the rope
x: The particles of the rope vibrate up and down about their mean positions while the disturbance travels along the rope. They do not travel with the wave.

q: In which of the following does sound travel fastest?
x: Sound generally travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases. It cannot travel at all in a vacuum.

q: Two sources of waves are said to be coherent when they have:
o: The same wavelength but a randomly changing phase
The same frequency and a constant phase difference
x: Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a phase difference that stays constant in time. Only then does a steady interference pattern form.

q: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude that:
o: Travel at right angles to each other
Have a constant phase difference of π/2 and travel together
x: A stationary (standing) wave arises when two identical progressive waves travel through the same medium in opposite directions, for example an incident and a reflected wave.

q: A long spring (slinky) lying on a smooth table is pushed and pulled repeatedly along its length at one end. The wave produced consists of:
o: Compressions and rarefactions moving along the spring
Crests and troughs moving along the spring
Coils moving permanently towards the far end
A single pulse that stays at the hand
x: Pushing and pulling along the length bunches the coils together (compressions) and spreads them apart (rarefactions); these regions travel along the spring as a longitudinal wave. Crests and troughs belong to transverse waves.

q: The speed of sound in a medium is given by v = √(E/ρ), where ρ is the density. Here E stands for:
o: The energy of the sound wave
The modulus of elasticity of the medium
x: Newton showed that the speed of sound depends on the elasticity (modulus E) and density ρ of the medium: v = √(E/ρ). It does not depend on the wave's energy or amplitude.

q: Two loudspeakers are driven by two separate oscillators set to nominally the same frequency. A fixed pattern of loud and quiet points is not obtained because:
o: The phase difference between the two sources does not stay constant
The amplitudes of the two waves are always equal
x: Two independent oscillators are never exactly matched, so their phase difference keeps drifting. The sources are not coherent and the loud and quiet points keep moving.

q: Which statement about a stationary wave is correct?
o: It carries energy along the medium at the wave speed
All its particles vibrate with the same amplitude
There is no net transfer of energy along the medium
Particles in all its segments vibrate in the same phase
x: In a stationary wave energy is stored and shuttles locally between kinetic and potential forms; there is no net flow along the medium. Amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes.

q: A single sharp up-and-down jerk is given to one end of a stretched rope. What is produced?
o: A pulse that travels along the rope
A stationary wave with fixed nodes
A longitudinal wave along the rope
x: A single disturbance produces a single pulse that moves along the rope. A continuous periodic wave needs the end to be moved up and down continuously.

q: In deriving his formula for the speed of sound in air, Newton assumed that the compressions and rarefactions take place:
x: Newton assumed the temperature of the air stays constant as sound passes, i.e. an isothermal process. Laplace later corrected this to adiabatic.

q: Two coherent waves of amplitudes 3 mm and 5 mm arrive at a point exactly in phase. The amplitude of the resultant wave at that point is:
x: In phase, the displacements add at every instant, so the resultant amplitude is 3 + 5 = 8 mm. 2 mm would be the result for waves in opposite phase.

q: Two particles of a stationary wave lie in adjacent loops, one on each side of a node. The phase difference between their vibrations is:
x: All particles within one loop (between two adjacent nodes) move in phase, while particles in adjacent loops move in opposite phase, a phase difference of π.

q: A small ribbon is tied to the middle of a long stretched rope. As a transverse wave passes along the rope, the ribbon:
o: Moves along the rope to the far end
Vibrates up and down but stays at the same place along the rope
Moves back towards the hand that is shaking the rope
x: The ribbon moves with the rope particle it is tied to, which only vibrates about its mean position. The wave passes on, but the ribbon does not travel along the rope.

q: According to Newton's formula, the speed of sound in a gas of pressure P and density ρ is:
x: Newton took the elastic modulus of a gas equal to its pressure, giving v = √(P/ρ). The formula with γ is Laplace's corrected version.

q: At a point of constructive interference between waves from two coherent sources:
o: A crest falls on a crest and a trough on a trough
A crest always falls on a trough
The two waves have different frequencies
The resultant displacement is always zero
x: Constructive interference means the waves arrive in phase: crest meets crest and trough meets trough, giving maximum amplitude. Crest on trough gives destructive interference.

q: How does the amplitude of the particles in a stationary wave compare with that in a progressive wave?
o: In a stationary wave it varies from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes; in a progressive wave it is the same for all particles
It is the same for all particles in both waves
In a progressive wave it varies from point to point; in a stationary wave it is the same for all particles
It is zero for all particles of a stationary wave
x: In a progressive wave every particle vibrates with the same amplitude. In a stationary wave the amplitude depends on position: zero at nodes, maximum at antinodes.

q: A student shakes the end of a stretched rope with a larger up-and-down movement of the hand, keeping the rate of shaking the same. Which property of the wave increases?
x: A bigger movement of the source gives a bigger maximum displacement, i.e. a larger amplitude. Frequency is set by the rate of shaking and speed by the rope, so the wavelength does not change either.

q: Newton took the elastic (bulk) modulus of air to be equal to its pressure P. Which law did he apply to get this result?
x: For an isothermal change Boyle's law (PV = constant) gives the bulk modulus E = P. The adiabatic law gives E = γP, which is Laplace's correction.

q: Two coherent waves of equal amplitude meet in phase at a point. Compared with the intensity of one wave alone, the intensity at that point is:
x: The resultant amplitude is doubled, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so intensity becomes 2² = 4 times. Twice comes from forgetting to square.

q: On a string fixed at both ends, the two waves that superpose to form the stationary wave are:
o: Two waves from two different vibrators at each end
The incident wave and the wave reflected from the fixed end
A transverse wave and a longitudinal wave
A wave on the string and a sound wave in the air
x: A wave sent along the string is reflected at the fixed end and travels back. The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and amplitude and travel in opposite directions, forming a stationary wave.

q: A student shakes a stretched rope up and down twice as often per second, without changing the tension in the rope. Which statement about the new wave is correct?
o: Its speed doubles and its wavelength stays the same
Its wavelength halves and its speed stays the same
Its frequency and wavelength both double
Its speed and frequency both halve
x: The wave speed depends on the rope and its tension, so it stays the same. Since v = fλ, doubling f halves λ.

q: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and density 1.6 kg m⁻³. Using Newton's formula, the speed of sound in it is:
x: v = √(P/ρ) = √(1.0 × 10⁵ / 1.6) = √62 500 = 250 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 62 500.

q: For two waves of wavelength λ, a path difference of λ/4 corresponds to a phase difference of:
x: Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference = (2π/λ) × (λ/4) = π/2. A full wavelength of path difference corresponds to 2π.

q: Two progressive waves, each of amplitude 2 mm, travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave. The amplitude of vibration at an antinode is:
x: At an antinode the two waves always arrive in phase, so the displacements add: 2 + 2 = 4 mm. Zero is the amplitude at a node.

q: One end of a slinky spring lying on a table is moved quickly from side to side, across the length of the spring. The wave produced is:
o: Longitudinal, because the coils move perpendicular to the direction of travel
Transverse, because the coils move parallel to the direction of travel
Longitudinal, because the coils move parallel to the direction of travel
Transverse, because the coils move perpendicular to the direction of travel
x: Moving the end sideways makes the coils vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, so the wave is transverse. A slinky gives a longitudinal wave only when pushed and pulled along its length.

q: The bulk modulus of water is 2.25 × 10⁹ Pa and its density is 1000 kg m⁻³. Using v = √(E/ρ), the speed of sound in water is:
Two coherent sound sources vibrate in antiphase (phase difference π). At a point that is exactly the same distance from both sources, the sound is:
o: A minimum, because the waves arrive in opposite phase
A maximum, because the path difference is zero
A maximum, because the sources are coherent
x: With zero path difference the waves keep the phase difference they started with, which is π. They arrive in opposite phase and interfere destructively.

q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. What is its speed?
x: v = fλ = 50 × 4 = 200 m s⁻¹. Dividing f by λ instead of multiplying gives 12.5 m s⁻¹.

q: The amplitude of a progressive wave is made three times as large, its frequency staying the same. Its intensity becomes:
x: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so I becomes 3² = 9 times as large. Forgetting to square gives 3 times.

q: A sound wave of frequency 680 Hz travels in air at 340 m s⁻¹. What is the distance between a compression and the rarefaction next to it?
x: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.5 m; a compression and the next rarefaction are half a wavelength apart, 0.25 m. Giving the full wavelength, 0.5 m, is the usual slip.

q: Two points on the path of a progressive wave of frequency 500 Hz are 0.2 m apart and vibrate with a phase difference of π/2. What is the speed of the wave?
x: Phase difference = 2πΔx/λ, so π/2 = 2π(0.2)/λ and λ = 0.8 m; v = fλ = 500 × 0.8 = 400 m s⁻¹. Taking π/2 as half a wavelength gives λ = 0.4 m and 200 m s⁻¹.

q: The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹ at 27 °C. Taking the speed as proportional to √T, with T in kelvin, at what temperature is the speed 680 m s⁻¹?
x: Doubling v needs T to be 4 times as large: 4 × 300 K = 1200 K = 927 °C. Doubling T instead gives 600 K = 327 °C; leaving the answer in kelvin gives 1200.

q: Newton's formula gives the speed of sound in air as 280 m s⁻¹. Laplace replaced P by γP, with γ = 1.44 for air. What speed does Laplace's formula give?
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √γ × √(P/ρ) = 1.2 × 280 = 336 m s⁻¹. Multiplying by γ itself instead of √γ gives 403 m s⁻¹.

q: The pressure of the air in a closed room is doubled while its temperature is kept constant. The speed of sound in the room:
x: v = √(γP/ρ); at constant temperature the density doubles along with the pressure, so P/ρ and the speed do not change. Looking only at P in the formula gives √2 times.

q: The speed of sound in oxygen (molar mass 32 g mol⁻¹) is 320 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of sound in hydrogen (molar mass 2 g mol⁻¹) at the same temperature and pressure? Both gases are diatomic.
x: Same γ and P, so v ∝ 1/√ρ, and ρ ∝ molar mass: v_H = 320 × √(32/2) = 320 × 4 = 1280 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 5120 m s⁻¹; inverting the ratio gives 80 m s⁻¹.

q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard per second?
x: Beat frequency = difference of the frequencies = 260 − 256 = 4 per second. 258 Hz is the average frequency of the sound heard, not the beat rate.

q: Fork X has a frequency of 384 Hz. Sounded with fork Y it gives 6 beats per second. When Y is loaded with a little wax, the beats fall to 4 per second. The original frequency of Y is:
x: Y is 384 ± 6 Hz, that is 390 Hz or 378 Hz. Wax lowers Y's frequency; the beats fall only if Y was above 384 Hz, so Y = 390 Hz. If Y were 378 Hz, loading would make the beats more frequent.

q: Two coherent sources vibrating in phase emit waves of wavelength 0.4 m. Point P is 2.0 m from one source and 2.6 m from the other. At P there is:
o: A maximum, because both distances are whole multiples of 0.2 m
An intermediate amplitude, between a maximum and a minimum
x: Path difference = 2.6 − 2.0 = 0.6 m = 1.5λ, a half-odd number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in antiphase and cancel: a minimum. A maximum needs a whole number of wavelengths.

q: Two coherent waves of amplitudes 3 mm and 1 mm interfere. What is the ratio of the maximum intensity to the minimum intensity in the pattern?
x: Amax = 3 + 1 = 4 mm and Amin = 3 − 1 = 2 mm; intensity ∝ A², so Imax/Imin = 16/4 = 4. Not squaring gives 2; 9 is the ratio of the two separate intensities.

q: In a stationary wave the distance between two neighbouring nodes is 15 cm. What is the wavelength of the wave?
x: Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart, so λ = 2 × 15 = 30 cm. Taking the node spacing as the whole wavelength gives 15 cm.

q: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends. Waves travel along it at 240 m s⁻¹. What is its fundamental frequency?
x: In the fundamental the string length is λ/2, so f₁ = v/2L = 240/2.4 = 100 Hz. Forgetting the 2 gives 200 Hz; using the closed-pipe 4L gives 50 Hz.

q: A pipe 0.5 m long is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of its first overtone?
x: Fundamental f₁ = v/4L = 340/2 = 170 Hz. A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so the first overtone is 3f₁ = 510 Hz. Taking 2f₁ = 340 Hz, as for an open pipe, is the tempting slip.

q: The tension in a stretched string is made four times as large, its length and mass staying the same. Its fundamental frequency:
x: f₁ = v/2L and v = √(T/m), so f ∝ √T: four times the tension gives twice the frequency. Forgetting the square root gives four times.

q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. How many nodes are there along it, counting the two fixed ends?
x: The third harmonic has 3 loops; 3 loops need 4 nodes, including the two ends, with 3 antinodes between them. 3 is the number of antinodes.

q: A train moving at constant speed straight towards a stationary listener sounds its whistle. While it approaches, the listener hears:
o: A constant frequency lower than the whistle's actual frequency
A constant frequency higher than the whistle's actual frequency
A frequency that keeps rising as the train gets closer
x: For a source approaching at constant speed, f′ = fv/(v − us) is constant and greater than f. The frequency does not keep rising; it drops suddenly only when the train passes.

q: A siren of frequency 600 Hz moves at 40 m s⁻¹ straight towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the observer hear?
x: Source moving towards: f′ = fv/(v − us) = 600 × 340/300 = 680 Hz. Using the moving-observer formula 600 × 380/340 gives 671 Hz.

q: A cyclist rides at 34 m s⁻¹ straight towards a stationary horn of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the cyclist hear?
x: Observer moving towards: f′ = f(v + u₀)/v = 500 × 374/340 = 550 Hz. Using the moving-source formula 500 × 340/306 gives 556 Hz; 450 Hz is for moving away.

q: A source of sound of frequency 720 Hz moves at 20 m s⁻¹ straight away from a stationary listener. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the listener hear?
x: Source moving away: f′ = fv/(v + us) = 720 × 340/360 = 680 Hz. Using v − us gives 765 Hz (approach); using the observer formula 720 × 320/340 gives 678 Hz.

q: A car horn moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is heard at 720 Hz by a roadside listener while the car approaches. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the listener hear after the car has passed and is moving away?
x: Approach: 720 = f × 340/320, so f = 677.6 Hz. Receding: f′ = f × 340/360 = 720 × 320/360 = 640 Hz. 678 Hz is the horn's actual frequency, not what is heard.

q: A stationary observer hears a frequency 1.25 times the actual frequency of a source moving straight towards him. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of the source?
x: v/(v − us) = 1.25 gives 340 − us = 272, so us = 68 m s⁻¹. Using the moving-observer formula (v + u)/v = 1.25 gives 85 m s⁻¹; 272 m s⁻¹ is v − us, not us.

q: A source of frequency 330 Hz and an observer move straight towards each other, each at 10 m s⁻¹ relative to still air. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the observer hear?
x: f′ = f(v + u₀)/(v − us) = 330 × 350/330 = 350 Hz. Allowing for only one of the two motions gives about 340 Hz; 311 Hz is for moving apart.

q: A police radar gun finds the speed of a car by measuring:
o: The change in frequency of the radio waves reflected from the car
The time the reflected waves take to return
The change in speed of the radio waves after reflection
The loudness of the car's engine
x: Waves reflected from a moving car come back with a Doppler-shifted frequency; the size of the shift gives the car's speed. The speed of the radio waves does not change.

q: The spectral lines in the light from a distant galaxy are found at longer wavelengths than the same lines measured in the laboratory. This shows that the galaxy is:
o: At rest relative to the Earth
x: A shift to longer wavelength (red shift) means the source is receding; an approaching source gives a blue shift. Temperature does not shift the positions of the lines.

q: A spectral line of wavelength 600 nm in the laboratory is observed at 606 nm in the light from a star. Using Δλ/λ = v/c with c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the star is moving:
o: Towards the Earth at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
Away from the Earth at 3 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹
Away from the Earth at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
Away from the Earth at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
x: Δλ/λ = 6/600 = 0.01, so v = 0.01 × 3 × 10⁸ = 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹; the wavelength has increased, so the star is receding. A longer wavelength does not mean approach.

q: A source of frequency 500 Hz moves at 40 m s⁻¹ through still air, where sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength of the sound in front of the source?
x: In front, the waves are crowded: λ′ = (v − us)/f = 300/500 = 0.60 m. 0.68 m is the wavelength from a stationary source and 0.76 m is the wavelength behind it.
